solutions.check: bars rebuilt from the blog's numbered answers (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Catholic young woman mostly seen in Covent Garden

indicators.note: something seen in a place sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other

parts.note: the Royal Opera House stands in Covent Garden, London

indicators.note: mostly means not quite all, so the final letter of the word is lopped off

parts.note: a miss is a girl or young unmarried woman

explanation.surface: A young Catholic woman spotted among the market stalls and street performers of London's Covent Garden.
explanation.walkthrough: Covent Garden is the London district housing the Royal Opera House, and crosswords use its initials for the place.
explanation.definitionFit: Romish is a dated, often disparaging adjective for things relating to the Roman Catholic Church.

clue.text: Ringing about native worker

parts.note: re means concerning
a native of a place is a son of it, as in native son
the worker ant is the crossword's usual worker

explanation.surface: A phone call concerning a local labourer.
explanation.definitionFit: Resonant sound is echoing and vibrating, so it means ringing out.

clue.text: Fish over on Maori settlement

parts.note: O is the cricket-scoring abbreviation for an over
a pa or pah is a fortified Maori village

explanation.surface: Fish caught above a village in New Zealand.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' puts the first piece above the second.
explanation.definitionFit: The opah or moonfish is a large brightly coloured deep-sea fish.

clue.text: Lime's out with one aged group of trees

indicators.note: is out means put out of order, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written, to be jumbled
an ace is a one in cards and dice
ae, short for aetatis, means aged, as on gravestones

explanation.surface: The lime tree is excluded from a family that includes one old tree group.
explanation.walkthrough: The lime of the surface is in fact unrelated to this family; only its letters are used.
explanation.definitionFit: Meliaceae is the mahogany family of tropical trees and shrubs, a botanical grouping.

clue.text: Last to have drink outside in parody

indicators.note: outside means wrapping round, so the drink encloses the other piece

parts.note: to sup is to drink
the last part is the end

explanation.surface: A comic take on someone finishing a pint outdoors.
explanation.definitionFit: A send-up is a satirical imitation, which is exactly what a parody is.

clue.text: My pet piddled in Roman venue

indicators.note: piddled suggests messed about, so the letters that follow are jumbled

parts.note: taken as written, to be jumbled

explanation.surface: Someone's pet dog relieved itself in an ancient Roman arena.
explanation.walkthrough: 'My pet' reads as an animal, but it is an endearment.
explanation.definitionFit: Mavourneen is an Irish term of endearment meaning my darling, from Irish mo mhuirnín.

clue.text: Fine ship coming from US city

parts.note: F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine
the Argo was Jason's ship in Greek myth

explanation.surface: A splendid vessel has sailed in from an American port.
explanation.definitionFit: Fargo is the largest city in North Dakota, also known from the Coen brothers film.

clue.text: One close friend initially suffered reverse in ligaments

indicators.note: a reverse is a setback, but read literally the pieces run backwards

parts.note: a means one
near means close by

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letter is used

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A close friend took a setback involving torn ligaments.
explanation.definitionFit: Fraena, plural of fraenum, are small folds of tissue such as the one tying the tongue, akin to ligaments.

clue.text: Working with latitude in part

indicators.note: in part means only a portion of the word is used, a run of letters inside it

parts.note: the letters sit inside the word

explanation.surface: Busy with some measure of freedom.
explanation.definitionFit: Being at it is an idiom for being busy, working away at something.

clue.text: Fancy long beer in French city

indicators.note: fancy as an adjective means elaborate or made-up, so the letters are reworked

parts.note: taken as written, to be jumbled

explanation.surface: Wanting a long drink of beer somewhere in France.
explanation.definitionFit: Grenoble is a city in the French Alps, in the Isère department.

clue.text: Ancient cut head off with blades

indicators.note: cutting off the head means losing the opening letter

parts.note: hoary means very old

explanation.surface: An old man is beheaded with swords.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'blades' of the surface are weapons; in the answer they are the flat ends of oars.
explanation.definitionFit: Oary is a poetic adjective meaning having oars or oar-like, and the oar's flat end is its blade.

clue.text: Cross and rather disturbed about North American edentates

parts.note: a cross is written as the letter X

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the jumbled letters wrap round another piece
disturbed things are thrown out of their settled order, so these letters get rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be jumbled
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Someone angry and somewhat upset about North American toothless mammals.
explanation.walkthrough: The jumble of the word rather is split open so the two-letter abbreviation sits after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Xenarthra is the zoological superorder of sloths, anteaters and armadillos, once classed as edentates for their reduced teeth.

clue.text: Marine creature found in smack getting load switched

indicators.note: the alternate letters of the word load are to be swapped round, a two-letter exchange inside the word

parts.note: a smack is a slap

explanation.surface: A sea animal turns up inside a fishing smack after the cargo has been shifted around.
explanation.walkthrough: Take alternate letters of load, L and A, and switch them inside SLAP. A smack is also a fishing boat, which is what the surface wants you to see.
explanation.definitionFit: A salp is a free-floating barrel-shaped tunicate found in the open sea.

clue.text: Insect's trapped so I help out with flowers

indicators.note: something trapped is held inside, so one piece goes within the other
out here means out of order, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written, to be jumbled
the usual crossword insect

explanation.surface: A bug is caught in the bouquet, so I help get it out.
explanation.definitionFit: Polianthes is the plant genus that includes the tuberose, prized for its fragrant flowers.

clue.text: Comparatively thoughtless climber runs around highest in range

indicators.note: around means encircling, so the climber with runs wraps round a further letter

parts.note: a vine is a climbing plant
R is the cricket-scoring abbreviation for runs
A is the top grade in a range of marks

explanation.surface: A mountaineer, rather careless, scrambles about near the top of the mountain range.
explanation.walkthrough: A, the top grade, goes inside VINE+R. The surface 'climber' and 'range' both point to mountains, but the climber is a plant.
explanation.definitionFit: Vain can mean foolish or empty-headed, so vainer is the comparative of that unthinking sense.

clue.text: Rustic loves religious type in India

parts.note: a hind is an old word for a farm labourer or peasant
love is zero in tennis, written O; two of them

explanation.surface: A country bumpkin is fond of a particular Indian faith.
explanation.definitionFit: Hindoo is an old spelling of Hindu, a follower of the main religion of India.

clue.text: Cravat seen in line before church

parts.note: stein, also steen, is an old verb meaning to line a well with stone
kirk is Scots for church

explanation.surface: A neckcloth spotted in a queue outside a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Line' is not a queue but the verb: Chambers gives stein for lining with stone. 'Before' just places the first piece first.
explanation.definitionFit: A steinkirk was a loosely tied lace neckcloth of around 1700, named after the Battle of Steenkerque.

clue.text: Took as before without a bit of authority — that's distraint

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so one piece wraps round the other

parts.note: an archaic past tense of nim, to take

indicators.note: a bit of a word is a small piece of it, here its opening letter

parts.note: the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: Someone seized goods in the old way, lacking any official power, and that is distraint.
explanation.walkthrough: 'As before' flags an archaic form: NAM is an old past tense of nim, meaning take. 'Without' means outside, its older sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Naam is an old legal term for the seizure of goods to enforce payment, which is what distraint means.

clue.text: Poison perhaps behind bird's nest

parts.note: the arse is the behind, British slang
a nide is a nest or brood of pheasants

explanation.surface: Toxin probably tucked behind where the bird nests.
explanation.definitionFit: Arsenides are compounds of arsenic with another element, and many are poisonous, hence 'perhaps'.

clue.text: Empty street surrounded by University, almost nothing to be seen

indicators.note: something surrounded by others sits inside them
almost means not quite all, so the final letter of the word goes

parts.note: standard abbreviation
nowt is northern English dialect for nothing
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A deserted street near the campus, with hardly anything to be seen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Empty' looks like an adjective describing the street, but it is the verb defining the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To unstow is to empty out what has been packed or stowed away, such as a ship's hold.

clue.text: Furious with nothing inside except strong meat

parts.note: wild means very angry

indicators.note: inside places this letter within the following word

parts.note: bar means except, as in all bar one
O looks like zero

explanation.surface: Livid at being given only robust meat with nothing else in it.
explanation.definitionFit: Wild boar is a gamey, strongly flavoured meat from the wild pig.

clue.text: Erratic chap scratching 100 — he could hold you up

indicators.note: scratching a runner means withdrawing it, so this letter is taken out

parts.note: taken as written; the word also signals the jumble
taken as written
C is the Roman numeral for 100

explanation.surface: An unpredictable man crossing out a hundred, a robber who might hold you up.
explanation.walkthrough: Take one C out of ERRATIC CHAP and rearrange. 'Erratic' does double duty as fodder and as the only anagram signal, which the blog itself queried.
explanation.definitionFit: An archpirate is a chief pirate, and pirates hold up ships and their crews to rob them.

clue.text: Electoral malpractice upset one special command

parts.note: to eat someone is to upset or bother them, as in what's eating you
an is the indefinite article, meaning one
standard abbreviation
a will is a command or decree

explanation.surface: Rigging an election annoys one particular authority.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' looks like an anagram signal, but it simply means EAT, as in bother. Eatanswill is the town in Dickens's Pickwick Papers with a notoriously corrupt election.
explanation.definitionFit: Chambers lists Eatanswill, from the corrupt election in Pickwick Papers, as a byword for electoral corruption.

clue.text: Well-behaved prisoner and copper on time

parts.note: standard abbreviation
rusty is a reddish-brown, copper-coloured shade

explanation.surface: A model inmate and a police officer are on time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' reads as a policeman, but it is a colour.
explanation.definitionFit: A trusty is a prisoner trusted with privileges for good behaviour.

clue.text: Sister takes against musical instrument

indicators.note: takes means holds within, so one word goes inside the other

parts.note: SR is the abbreviation for Sister
anti means opposed to

explanation.surface: A nun objects to some kind of instrument.
explanation.definitionFit: A santir is a Persian hammered dulcimer, a stringed musical instrument.

clue.text: Each in rotation gets a container

indicators.note: in places one piece inside another

parts.note: a turn is a rotation
EA is the shopping abbreviation for each

explanation.surface: Everyone taking turns gets a pot to hold things.
explanation.definitionFit: A tea urn is a large metal vessel with a tap, used to hold and dispense hot water or tea.

clue.text: Cut and cut extremely stupid returns

indicators.note: returns means comes back the way it went, so the letters run backwards
cut at the extremity means trimming the end, so the final letter goes

parts.note: dense means slow-witted

explanation.surface: A very stupid cut comes back again.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' appears twice: first as the definition, then as the signal to clip the end of DENSE.
explanation.definitionFit: Sned is a Scots and dialect verb meaning to lop or prune, so it is a synonym of cut.

clue.text: Maid's served up meat after one

parts.note: a means one

indicators.note: in a down clue up means read from bottom to top

parts.note: ham is a meat

explanation.surface: A servant has dished up meat after someone.
explanation.definitionFit: An amah is a nursemaid or maidservant in East or South Asia.

clue.text: Poet's twisted humour holding centre of attention

indicators.note: holding means containing, so one piece goes inside the other

parts.note: wit is humour

indicators.note: centre of means the middle letter of the word

parts.note: the middle letter of the word

explanation.surface: A writer's warped comedy keeps the focus of attention.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poet's' flags a literary word: Spenser uses wint as a past form of wind, to turn.
explanation.definitionFit: Wint is a Spenserian past tense of wind, meaning wound or turned, so twisted in old verse.

clue.text: Prince in this country with good plan gets backing

indicators.note: backing means moving in reverse, so the whole string is read from the end

parts.note: this country is the UK, from the British setter's viewpoint
standard abbreviation
a net is a flat plan that folds into a solid shape

explanation.surface: A royal in Britain with a sound scheme wins support.
explanation.walkthrough: A net in geometry is the flat pattern that folds up into a solid, so it serves as a plan.
explanation.definitionFit: Tengku is a Malay title for a prince or member of a royal family.

clue.text: Press well up on getting leader sacked

indicators.note: the leader is the front letter, and sacking it removes it

parts.note: to surge is to well up

explanation.surface: Journalists are excited when a boss is fired.
explanation.definitionFit: To press someone is to urge them, so the two verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Make less money for female in the end

indicators.note: for here means in place of, so one letter stands in where another was

parts.note: standard abbreviation
standard abbreviation
the finish is the end

explanation.surface: Cut pay for a woman in the long run.
explanation.walkthrough: In FINISH the F becomes M. The surface reads as a pay cut, but 'money for female' is the swap.
explanation.definitionFit: Minish is an archaic verb meaning to diminish, so it means to reduce or make smaller.

clue.text: Artist coming from Russian commune with nothing

parts.note: a mir was a Russian peasant village community
O looks like zero

explanation.surface: A painter emerges from a Soviet collective empty-handed.
explanation.definitionFit: Joan Miró was a Spanish Catalan painter and sculptor associated with Surrealism.

clue.text: A force on European border for the present

parts.note: taken as written
dint means force, as in by dint of
standard abbreviation
a rim is an edge or border

explanation.surface: An army stationed on a European frontier for the time being.
explanation.definitionFit: Ad interim is Latin for meanwhile, used of temporary arrangements that hold until something permanent.

clue.text: Rather heavy newspaper with aspiration, according to reporter!

parts.note: aspiration is the breathy sound written H

indicators.note: a reporter here is someone speaking, so the letters are taken by their sound

parts.note: the FT, the Financial Times, said as its letters

explanation.surface: A weighty newspaper with lofty ambitions, as a journalist might say.
explanation.walkthrough: Say the initials FT aloud and put an H sound before them. 'Aspiration' means ambition on the surface but here is the breathed H.
explanation.definitionFit: Hefty means large and heavy, so it fits as a synonym for fairly weighty.

clue.text: One pushing for cut not a little loud

parts.note: pro means in favour of

indicators.note: not means without, so the following letter is removed

parts.note: a kerf is the cut made by a saw
F, forte, is the musical marking for loud, a small letter

explanation.surface: Someone who campaigns in favour of cuts, but not too noisily.
explanation.walkthrough: A kerf is the slit a saw leaves; drop its F (forte, loud in music).
explanation.definitionFit: A proker is a Scots or dialect word for a poker, the rod used to push and stir a fire.
